The words

In God's own house pronounce his praise,
His grace he there reveals;
To heaven your joy and wonder raise,
For there his glory dwells.

Let all your sacred passions move,
While you rehearse his deeds;
But the great work of saving love
Your highest praise exceeds.

All that have motion, life, and breath,
Proclaim your Maker blest;
Yet when my voice expires in death,
My soul shall praise him best.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (F), on the word “In”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719): Psalm 150, headed “A song of praise”.

Watts' psalms were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Common Metre (8.6.8.6). This page sets the words to WINCHESTER OLD; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1719): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Music (Whole Book of Psalmes, 1592): Thomas Este (died undefined)
  • Arranged (tenor lead): George Kirbye (died 1634)

Questions about In God's Own House Pronounce His Praise

What is the doh of In God's Own House Pronounce His Praise?

In this version, in F major, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does In God's Own House Pronounce His Praise start on?

It starts on d (F in F major), a pickup on the word “In” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is In God's Own House Pronounce His Praise in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Thomas Este died in undefined, George Kirbye died in 1634; the words were first published in 1719 and the music in 1592. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
